t: Find the Integer Added to Array II
o: Two elements were deleted from nums1 and every remaining element shifted by a single unknown integer x, producing nums2 (as multisets). We must recover the minimum valid x. Since exactly two elements were removed, the smallest element of sorted nums2 must match one of the three smallest elements of sorted nums1 — so x ∈ {b[0]−a[0], b[0]−a[1], b[0]−a[2]} for sorted arrays a, b. Each candidate is verified by greedily matching sorted nums2 against sorted nums1 with exactly two skips. Example 1: sorted a=[4,8,12,16,20], b=[10,14,18]; candidates give x=−2 (matching 12,16,18→10,14,18 after removing 4 and 20), the minimum. Example 2: a=[3,3,5,5], b=[7,7], x=2 works by removing both 3s.
k: Only three candidate shifts exist: b_sorted[0] − a_sorted[i] for i = 0,1,2, because the smallest kept element of nums1 is among its three smallest.
Verify a candidate by merging sorted arrays and requiring exactly two unmatched elements in nums1 and full consumption of nums2.
Take the minimum verified candidate; the problem guarantees at least one exists.

a.i: Sorting both arrays turns multiset equality into sequence matching. For a hypothesized x, walk sorted nums1 and advance through sorted nums2 whenever nums1[i] + x equals the current nums2[j]; every non-match is a 'removed' element. Validity requires exactly two removals and all of nums2 consumed. Trying the three possible anchors of b[0] covers all cases with O(n) verification each.
s: For i in 0..2, set x = nums2[0] − nums1[i].
Verify x with a linear merge allowing exactly two skips; keep the smallest valid x.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; three verifications are O(n) each.

a.i: With n ≤ 200 one can also enumerate which two elements of nums1 are removed — O(n²) pairs — shift the rest by x = nums2_min − kept_min, and compare multisets directly. Slower and clunkier, but completely foolproof and useful as a correctness cross-check or when the 'two removals' structure were different.
s: For each pair (p, q), p < q, build the multiset of nums1 minus indices p and q.
Derive x from the difference of minimums and check multiset equality with nums2 after shifting.
a.t: O(n³) in the worst case (n² pairs × O(n) multiset check) — fine for n ≤ 200 but far from optimal.

w: Use Approach 1 — the 'only three candidates' argument is elegant and interviewers love it: after sorting, the minimum of nums2 must align with one of the first three elements of nums1. Pitfalls: x may be negative (Example 1), so don't assume positivity; remember 'minimum x' means numerically smallest, not fewest operations; and verification must respect multiplicities (hence sorted matching, not sets). Follow-ups: k removals instead of two (k+1 candidates, same verification), or recovering x when multiple shifts are valid and you must report all.
